Nearly a third of top VPNs are secretly owned by Chinese companies, while other owners are based in countries with weak or no privacy laws, potentially putting users at risk, security researchers warn

Warwick Ashford

Security Editor

Almost a third (30%) of the world’s top virtual private network (VPN) providers are secretly owned by six Chinese companies, according to a study by privacy and security research firm VPNpro.

I will say that mine, and most other VPN services, promote their products as being end-to--end encryption. Meaning the work on your machine is encrypted before being sent, then sent through a vendor proxy server and on to a targeted vendor server of user choice/location before being unencrypted. The receiving server only knows the proxy server as the source of the transaction. And, the proxy server cannot read the encrypted data (if what they say is true), it simply passes it through to the targeted server, all before a request is made of the internet at large. Thus, the only thing any attacker might see is the target server info. IF the service itself is not doing that, then there's even bigger problems than your service possibly obtaining your data.

Supposedly, most/many have "no logging" of any activity, so even if legal request for info arrive, they have nothing to offer.
